newsitem.title: USA: Shopping for wine -- it's a matter of taste, not hype.
newsitem.headline: Shopping for wine -- it's a matter of taste, not hype.

text.p: A Latin proverb holds "In vino veritas" -- In wine is truth. But for many, the truth is -- buying wine is a big mystery.
You've got your reds, your whites, your French, your Spanish. Forget about all the Californias.

The number of wines available to the average consumer is daunting, and all of the hype and attitude surrounding the beverage has made the purchase of wine, which should be a simple task, often a Herculean one.

"Over all the rules, principles and guidelines, drink what you like and trust your own palate," said New York wine expert Joshua Wesson. "No one should tell you you're wrong," or that you're not spending enough.
But, yikes! There are hundreds of wines. How do you choose?
By asking yourself three easy questions, Wesson said, you can narrow down a 100 wine field to about four choices.
First, do you like red or white? Immediately the world of wine has been cut in half.
Second, do you like fizzy or flat? Third, do you like sweet or dry?
Depending on the answers to these questions, a wine shopper can winnow down the world of wine, with a sales person's help if necessary, to a manageable few from which to make the final choice.
"These are filters. You send wines you are not interested in out of world view," said Wesson, co-owner of Best Cellars Inc., a New York wine shop that specialises in "great wines under $10."
Stop worrying about the country of origin. Gone are the days when only the best wines were French, and California was synonymous with jug wines for fraternity parties.
Likewise, "Bulgaria, Italy or Spain may have been a pejorative 20 years ago, but now it's a moniker of quality," he said.

"Twenty to 40 years ago, France was said to produce a greater quality than the United States, but there's been a tremendous spread of wisdom around the world ... and an internationalization of wine making."

Take Champagne for example. The bubbly with a capital "C" comes from the Champagne region of France and is often priced at a premium, in part because the land there has gotten so expensive. However, the same grapes are now being grown elsewhere, and while the product can't be called "Champagne," it can be an equally high-quality sparkling wine.
Also, Wesson said, forget the old rule that pairs white wine with fish and red wine with meat.
"You can fall in love with someone just like you, or fall in love with someone who's a total opposite. It's the same with wines and foods," he said.
The once hard and fast rules have become flexible, although Wesson said there is some logic to them.
Fish, which has a pronounced flavor, is usually tempered with a squeeze of lemon. A fruity wine, often a white wine, will contain the right amount of acid, like lemon, to balance out fish.
Red meat, which gets its flavor from fat and blood, can be balanced by a wine rich in tannins, most often a red wine, which will leave an impression of sweetness.
But in the final analysis, it's about personal preference.
"It's not about colour coding. Bring your own palate preferences," he said.
A wine buyer should also not be afraid to have a preference for a beverage that comes in a "box."

"Wine doesn't know what kind of vessel it comes in, be it a box, can or keg. A glass bottle with a cork permits the slight exchange of oxygen and outside atmosphere - what's known as ageing," he said.
However, 90 percent of the world's wines do not benefit from ageing, Wesson said, and for this reason it's often wiser to purchase a younger wine rather than an older one.
The final deciding factor for purchasing a particular bottle of wine is price. Wesson said "there is a relationship between price and quality -- up to a point."
For wines that sell for $4 to $12 a bottle, generally speaking the $5 bottle will not taste as good as the $6 bottle, which will not be as good as the $7 one.

Above about $12 a bottle, "the law of diminishing returns kicks in." Up to about $20 a bottle, the relationship between price and quality becomes incremental, not monumental, as in the less expensive wines.
"You don't need to spend more than $10 to $12 (a bottle), and we prove this every day," Wesson said.
